slides.title: Your agency looks profitable — and still can't make payroll.
slides.body: Cash-flow gaps are the silent killer for new agencies. Here's how to forecast your way out of them before they hit.

slides.title: Revenue ≠ Cash in Hand
slides.body: You booked a $20k project. Great. But if the client pays net-60, you're funding six weeks of salaries, software, and contractor invoices out of pocket first. Always map when money actually arrives, not when it's earned.

slides.title: Build a 13-Week Rolling Forecast
slides.body: Forget annual projections for now. Track every expected inflow and outflow week by week for the next 13 weeks. Update it every Monday. Thirteen weeks is close enough to act on and far enough to see trouble coming.

slides.title: Know Your Three Cash Killers
slides.body: 1. Slow-paying clients on long net terms. 2. Contractor invoices due before client payment clears. 3. Uneven project starts — feast months followed by empty pipeline months. Label each one in your forecast so you can fix the right problem.

slides.title: The Retainer Fix Is Real — Here's Why
slides.body: A single $5k monthly retainer doesn't just add revenue. It adds a predictable inflow date you can plan around. Even one or two retainers dramatically smooths the spikes that make forecasting feel impossible.

slides.title: Set a Cash Reserve Rule on Day One
slides.body: Keep a minimum cash buffer equal to six weeks of fixed costs — payroll, tools, rent. Treat that number as untouchable. If your forecast dips below it, that's your trigger to chase invoices, pause spending, or accelerate a proposal.

slides.title: Save this and open it next Monday morning.
slides.body: Pull up your bank balance, list every payment due in and out over the next 13 weeks, and build your first forecast. One hour now will prevent a crisis later. Save this post so you don't lose the framework.

slides.title: Motivation Is A Lie (Here's What Actually Works)
slides.body: Everyone says "just stay motivated." But motivation is why most people quit. Here's the truth about building habits that actually stick.

slides.title: MYTH: You Need To Feel Motivated To Start
slides.body: Motivation follows action — it doesn't precede it. Waiting to feel ready is the fastest way to never begin. Consistency creates the feeling, not the other way around.

slides.title: MYTH: Motivated People Are More Disciplined
slides.body: Highly consistent people don't rely on willpower. They design their environment so the habit becomes the path of least resistance. Systems beat self-control every time.

slides.title: MYTH: Low Motivation Means Something Is Wrong With You
slides.body: Motivation naturally ebbs and flows — it's neurochemistry, not character. Treating it as a personal failure keeps you stuck in a shame spiral instead of a habit loop.

slides.title: MYTH: Big Goals Keep You Motivated Long-Term
slides.body: Big goals spike excitement and then fade. What keeps behavior going is a clear identity: "I am someone who does this" is more durable than "I want to achieve that."

slides.title: What Actually Builds Consistent Habits
slides.body:
→ Tiny starting points that feel almost too easy
→ A fixed time and trigger (not a feeling)
→ An identity tied to the behavior, not the outcome
→ Tracking streaks, not chasing inspiration

slides.title: Save This Before Your Motivation Runs Out
slides.body: Share this with someone who keeps waiting to feel ready. Follow for more no-fluff habit science every week.

test_case.input: Build a concise carousel for experienced product managers showing how to distinguish a weak customer signal from repeatable evidence. Include practical tests, avoid buzzwords, and end with an action the reader can take this week.
test_case.expected_behavior: Address experienced product managers with practical evidence tests, avoid buzzwords, and finish with an immediate action.

raw_output.title: Weak Signal or Real Evidence? A PM's Field Guide

slides.title: One customer complaint isn't a roadmap item
slides.body: But three is starting to look like a pattern. The difference between noise and signal is testable — here's how to tell them apart.

slides.title: The source problem
slides.body: A signal from your loudest account, your CEO's friend, or last week's churn call is not representative. Note who said it before you note what they said.

slides.title: The repetition test
slides.body: Has this problem surfaced across three or more unrelated customers, in their own words, without you prompting it? If you had to ask a leading question, the clock resets.

slides.title: The behavior gap test
slides.body: Did they describe a pain, or did they build a workaround? Workarounds are evidence. Complaints without action are wishes. Look for what people already do, not what they say they want.

slides.title: The specificity test
slides.body: Vague signals sound like 'it's hard to collaborate.' Real evidence sounds like 'every Monday I export this to a spreadsheet because the tool can't do X.' Precision is a proxy for frequency.

slides.title: The 'so what' test
slides.body: Ask: if we solved this, what metric moves and by how much? If no one can answer, the signal hasn't been stress-tested. Evidence survives this question. Noise doesn't.

slides.title: Run this test on one item in your backlog this week
slides.body: Pick a ticket backed by customer feedback. Apply all four tests. If it fails two or more, move it to a watch list — not the roadmap. Share what you find with your team.

Opens with a concrete, memorable threshold ('one vs. three') that immediately frames the problem for experienced PMs without condescension

It addresses experienced PMs with appropriate sophistication, avoids buzzwords entirely, and delivers genuinely differentiated practical tests rather than generic advice.
